Any attempted Bid assignment without GPC’s prior written consent will be void and the original Bidder will remain responsible for all its obligations relating to the Bid. GPC's consent to a proposed Bid Assignment will not create any obligation for GPC to the original Bidder or Bid Assignee beyond GPC's evaluation of the Bid according to the All-Source RFP. GPC reserves the right to reject a Bid Assignment in its sole but reasonable discretion, including if notice is late, incomplete, or GPC determines the Bid Assignment would be contrary to the All-Source RFP or the Commission’s orders relating to the All-Source RFP. If GPC rejects a Bidder’s proposed Bid Assignment, GPC will provide Bidder with notice through the IE, but the notice will not include a detailed explanation of GPC’s rejection of the Bid Assignment. GPC’s consent to any Bid assignment request is subject to, among other things, Bid Assignee’s acknowledgement of and agreement to the terms of the All-Source RFP, including the waiver in RFP Section 8.3 (Initial Review).

Exhibit G – Overview of Evaluation Methodology 
The following is a general overview of GPC’s methodology for Submission evaluation. PPA Bids, APA Bids, and any Company-Owned Proposal(s) will receive comparable evaluation that ensures a net total cost is calculated while accounting for the net present value of generation and transmission aspects over the life of the asset. As part of the evaluation, GPC may also consider the non-price factors described in Exhibit H (Non-Price Considerations).

All graphics and tables included in this Exhibit G (Overview of Evaluation Methodology) are for illustrative purposes only.

Net Total Cost Evaluation.
 The net total cost is the net present value of the generation and transmission aspects of the Submission in dollars per kilowatt ($/kW) of capacity contribution. The generation cost is comprised of both the fixed cost associated with the Submission and the variable cost associated with the operational parameters of the Submission, which will be used in production cost modeling simulations. The capacity contribution of each Submission will be based on the effective load carrying capability (“ELCC”), which will be determined by the process approved by the Commission in the 2022 IRP filed in Docket No. 44160. ELCC may vary based on technology type, operational characteristics within the same technology, and submission type. For example, ESS that differ in discharge duration may have different ELCC. For reference, the table below includes the current budget year ELCC values for incremental additions of ESS capacity of various durations for both standalone ESS and ESS with a new Renewable Resource that shares the same POI (e.g., excluding any Renewable Resource subject to an existing PPA with GPC).

Current Incremental ESS ELCC Values:
ESS Duration
Winter ELCC
4-hour
20%
6-hour
30%
8-hour
40%
10-hour
45%
12-hour
55%
Generation Costs – Determining Fixed Costs.

Fixed generation cost will include the following (as applicable to the Submission):

The Bidder-specified capacity cost payment (typically quoted in dollars per kilowatt ($/kW) for each year) for PPA Bids;
The costs associated with PPA treatment as either an Operating Lease or a Finance Lease, as applicable, if it is determined that the PPA constitutes a lease;
GPC’s revenue requirements for the purchase price for APA Bids and in-service costs for Company-Owned Proposals. These revenue requirements account for depreciation, cost of capital, and taxes; and
The fuel pipeline costs, which include the estimated costs for adequate firm natural gas transportation and natural gas storage, as applicable. This requirement is not applicable to an ESS Bid.

The evaluation will consider differences in the seasonal capability of each Submission.

Equity Cost of PPA – Determining the Balance Sheet Consequence for Operating Lease or Finance Lease Treatment.

If a Bid is determined to be a lease, there is an equity cost to GPC when the PPA is placed on GPC’s balance sheet caused by the Rating Agency treatment of a lease in accordance with FASB ASC Topic 842.

For a Finance Lease, GPC must capitalize the PPA as an asset on its balance sheet and must offset it by a debt obligation on the liability side of the balance sheet. The addition of the debt obligation on the balance sheet requires GPC to recapitalize to maintain the appropriate debt and equity ratio. As a result, there are direct equity costs incurred by GPC when a PPA is capitalized and reflected on the balance sheet as a Finance Lease. The equity cost of a Bid determined to result in a Finance Lease, if selected, will be evaluated by determining the net cost (lease cost less depreciation and tax implication) of capitalizing the PPA.

For an Operating Lease, the PPA is also added to the balance sheet but without directly affecting the debt and equity ratio on GPC’s books. However, rating agencies impute debt onto GPC’s balance sheet in their evaluation of the credit rating for GPC. Therefore, GPC must still recapitalize to maintain the target debt and equity ratio needed to ensure its credit rating is not impacted by the PPA. There is a direct equity cost premium associated with this treatment.

The additional annual revenue requirement cost to GPC is calculated for the Operating Lease or Finance Lease. The result is the equity cost applied to the Bid.

Generation Costs – Determining the Production Cost Savings.

The variable generation cost includes:
Fuel cost for any CT or CC Submission
Charging costs for any ESS Submission
Variable O&M
Facility dispatch characteristics
RECs and integration costs for ESS with Renewable Resource Submissions.
Production cost computer simulations are required to estimate the operational savings associated with operating each proposed Facility with the system dispatch. Each Submission’s contribution to reducing the aggregate annual system generation fleet fuel and variable cost can be calculated by comparing a cost simulation that includes the Submission against a reference simulation (without the Submission). The variable cost components of each Submission are modeled within the production cost simulation. In addition to fuel and O&M Costs, Facility operating characteristics, including efficiency (e.g., heat rate, Round-Trip Efficiency), scheduled maintenance requirements, any applicable Ancillary Services, and projected availability will contribute to the total production cost. For ESS Submissions, additional operating characteristics such as charge and discharge duration, cycle limits, and charging source (grid or paired resource) will contribute to calculation of the total production cost. 

Evaluation of ESS with Renewable Resource Submissions requires the renewable generation profile to be submitted for inclusion in the production cost simulation. There will be a $/MWh REC component attributed to any Renewable Energy to account for the forecasted value of RECs. Depending on the renewable generation technology and configuration of a paired ESS, a $/MWh integration cost will be applied to any Renewable Energy to account for costs arising from actions taken by system operators to respond to the additional volatility on the system from the intermittent nature of Renewable Resources. RECs and integration costs will be evaluated in accordance with the RCB Framework, as approved by the Commission in Docket 56002.

In general, GPC conducts the production cost simulation to calculate the projected annual production cost savings on a per kilowatt capacity basis for the Submission.

An illustrative example of the net generation cost calculation (total fixed generation costs net production cost savings) is provided below.
Evaluation Task:
Determine the Production Cost Savings


Net Generation Cost: Calculating the Net Generation Cost of a Proposal.

The production cost simulation is conducted to achieve the annual production cost savings. The calculation of the net generation cost for each proposal is a three-step process: (i) the Submission’s fixed costs are calculated annually on a dollar per kilowatt basis; (ii) on an annual basis, the per kilowatt production cost savings are subtracted from the fixed costs resulting in the annual net generation per kilowatt costs; and (iii) the final net generation cost is the accumulated net present value of the annual net generation costs.

An illustrative example of the net present value of the net generation cost calculation is provided in the following table.

Evaluation Task:
Determine the Present Value of the Net Generation Costs


Transmission Costs: Evaluation of Transmission Impacts of Bids.

An assessment of the transmission impact of each Submission will be an integral part of the net total cost analysis. Each Submission on the Competitive Tier is evaluated from a transmission network perspective to assess:
The additional network transmission investment required to deliver Facility output to native load on a firm basis; 
The additional network transmission investment required to provide grid charging service from the network, if applicable; and
The increase (or decrease) in transmission system energy losses due to the operation of the proposed Facility.

Each Submission is analyzed using transmission system computer simulation models to determine if additional transmission network improvements are required to accommodate the proposed Facility. For evaluation purposes, the Submission is assessed the yearly amortized cost of the transmission improvements. 
The transmission simulation models include future projections of transmission facilities and planned GPC-owned generation to maintain grid reliability in areas of major load (net of generation). 
In addition, each Submission is analyzed to determine whether operation of the proposed Facility increases or decreases the transmission system energy losses. Each Submission is assessed an annual cost (or credit) associated with its projected impact on the transmission system energy losses.
As part of the evaluation of transmission impacts of each Submission, GPC will further assess any project scheduling risk posed by the transmission system evaluation, including the ability of the proposed project to meet the RCOD or RCD, as applicable.
Illustrative examples of how the net transmission cost and net total cost are determined are provided below.

Due Diligence Portfolio Analysis

The Competitive Tier will be evaluated and ranked using a consistent methodology that identifies the best Submissions based on the net present value of net total cost per kW. To satisfy the capacity need targeted in this All-Source RFP, more than one Submission may be selected. A portfolio analysis will be required to determine the best portfolio (combination of two or more) of Submissions that satisfy the identified capacity need. For Submissions offering multiple units in a single Submission, each unit or group of units may be selected separately by GPC.

In the development of portfolios, the best Submissions will be packaged together into several combinations or “portfolios.” Each of the resulting portfolios will be evaluated using a net total cost approach that is consistent with the methodology used to evaluate each individual Submission. In the portfolio phase, a production cost simulation and a transmission cost analysis are required to evaluate the cost impacts resulting from any interaction that may result from packaging several Submissions into a portfolio.

Exhibit L – Facility Technical Requirements
Winterization Requirements
Each Submission must comply with the following requirements:
The Facility must comply with applicable EOP-012-3 (Extreme Cold Weather Preparedness and Operations) requirements, including Requirements R1 (applicable to New Facilities), R2 (applicable to Existing Facilities), R3, R4, R5, R6, and R7, and any successor reliability standard. EOP-012-3 is published by NERC and available at:  https://www.nerc.com/pa/Stand/Reliability%20Standards/EOP-012-3.pdf.     
Bidder must provide, by no later than Bid Due Date, the Facility’s: (i) extreme cold weather temperature; and (ii) cold weather preparedness plan.  
cybersecurity
Each Facility must comply with the requirements for Bulk Electric System generation facilities in North America set forth in the NERC reliability standards (Cyber Security Standards) created pursuant to FERC order 706 (Mandatory Reliability Standards for Critical Infrastructure Protection) and any other cyber security best practices consistent with Prudent Industry Practices. 
For all BESS Submissions, programmable electronic components of the: (i) Battery Management System (BMS); (ii) BESS Controller; and (iii) Site Controller (including controls, hardware, and software) must not be sourced from or manufactured by Foreign Entities of Concern as defined in 42 U.S.C. § 18741(5) and subsequently interpreted in “Interpretation of Foreign Entity of Concern,” 89 Fed. Reg. 37085 (May 6, 2024) or sourced from or manufactured in one of the following countries: China, Russia, North Korea, Saudi Arabia, Serbia, Algeria, Venezuela, Iran, Iraq, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Syria, Lebanon, South Sudan, Pakistan, or Cuba. For purposes of this provision, the terms Battery Management System, BESS Controller, and Site Controller are defined as follows:
Battery Management System (BMS): A control system used to protect the battery and to provide key parameters, such as state of charge, battery health, and temperature.
BESS Controller: A controller used to manage multiple stacks or arrays of batteries. This controller manages the balancing of the batteries.
Site Controller: A control system used to manage one or more sources (Photovoltaic solar, batteries, etc.) to achieve facility level control.
Additional Minimum Facility Technical Requirements FOR ESS FACILITIES 
PPA Bids for Facilities utilizing solar photovoltaic modules as a Renewable Resource must meet the following requirements:
Hydrology and Site drainage
Site grading must ensure positive drainage of the Site.
Site design must ensure no flooding, no standing water, and no increase in flows offsite.
The drainage design must be based on a 100-year, 24-hour rain event.
No portion of the Facility may be located in a floodplain without the proper permit(s) from the appropriate Governmental Authority.
The construction contract scope must include responsibility of contractor to close out the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permit.
Site grading and stabilization
Measures must be in place to prevent sediment loss.
Permanent site vegetation complying with the requirements of any authority having jurisdiction must be established and, if applicable, site stabilization must be completed before demobilizing.
Facility Design
Equipment must be sized to deliver rated Facility nameplate power at the POI, accounting for worst-case local ambient temperature, and interconnection reactive power requirement.
Site performance at the POI must meet the interconnection requirements as set forth by the Interconnection Provider.
Reactive power requirement must be solely met by the inverters without the use of capacitor banks.
All equipment enclosures (e.g., combiner boxes) must be tamperproof and lockable (e.g., a special tool or key is required to open the equipment enclosure).
Hurricane resistance rating and restoration plan.
Major Equipment Vendors 
Major equipment vendors must demonstrate quality and performance and be prepared to perform future warranty and maintenance work.
Major equipment must be manufactured in factories certified to both IEC TS 62941 and ISO 9001.
Final major equipment vendors subject to review by GPC.
PV Module
Solar modules must be sourced from Bloomberg New Energy Finance (BNEF) Tier 1 photovoltaic manufacturers.
Provide detailed Highly Accelerated Life Test (HALT) report (PVEL or equivalent) for the specific module proposed, preferably from independent third-party testing agency. 
Provide module manufacturing location and Bill of Material (BOM).
Inverter
Inverters must be listed to latest version of UL1741-SB.
Inverters may be reviewed by GPC.
Inverters must be capable of producing their maximum rated reactive power at all active power levels (from 0% to 100% inclusive), when the primary energy source is available and not available.
Inverters must be equipped with DC ground detection means through either insulation monitoring or differential current monitoring.
Facilities that are transmission interconnected must conform to NERC recommendations and requirements pertaining to IBR facilities.
Inverter Step-up Transformer
Transformers must be two-winding.
All transformers must be IEEE routinely tested including dielectric test, impulse test, and power factor test. Lightning impulse tests must include one full wave test.
Oil reservoir for spill containment must be provided for each transformer.
MV Switchgear
MV switchgear protection scheme must, at minimum, include main break protection, feeder breaker protection, bus differential protection, a dedicated bus lockout, and breaker failure functionality.
All current transformers must have an accuracy class of C400 or higher.
Grounding 
Dual grounding, as depicted in IEEE 665, must be provided in all cases with an equipment grounding conductor (for a reliable ground fault current return path) and an additional local safety ground (for limiting touch potential).
PV Monitoring
Meteorological and performance monitoring equipment/system must conform to IEC61724 and the requirements defined for a Class A (high) accuracy monitoring system.
Table 4 of IEC61724 will be used to determine the number of devices required. At minimum two devices of each measurement type must be provided.
At minimum two soiling stations utilizing full sized modules must be provided.
Testing
Operational test, performance ratio test, and Capacity test (ASTM Based) must be performed for PV facilities.
Additional testing, if required under the Interconnection Agreement, must also be performed.
NERC testing must be performed for facilities defined as a Bulk Electric System (BES).
Main Power Transformer
Transformers must be capable of meeting 100% of Facility output using 100% ONAF2-cooling.
Transformer suppliers may be subject to review.
RIS-type bushings are preferred.
Transformers must be designed with a 25% temporary emergency overload.
Transformer overload capability must be unlimited by components (i.e., bushing ratings, DETC rating, etc.) 
The transformer tank design must be in accordance with IEEE C57.156 Table 1 to mitigate tank rupture in the event of a high-energy arcing fault internal to the tank.
Facility Substation
Facility substations must meet safety requirements of the NESC-2023 and comply with the design principles set forth ASCE 7, ASCE 113, IEEE 605, and IEEE 80.
Facility substations must be commissioned to NETA ATS 17 standards.
All bus and cable sizes must be designed with a maximum operating temperature of 80 °C with a 40 °C ambient, with no sun and 2 ft/s wind.
Spatial separation from oil-filled electrical equipment must be compliant with IEEE 979-2012.
All equipment suppliers, protection and control designs and settings, and grounding design/modeling will be subject to review by GPC.
Cyber Security 
Facility connectivity must comply with NERC CIP policies.
End-of Life Disposal 
The Toxicity Characteristic Leaching Procedure (TCLP) testing procedure and results for modules must be submitted.
Description of the end-of-life disposal/recycling plan must be included.
PPA Bids for Facilities utilizing solar photovoltaic modules with an ESS comprised of a battery energy storage system (“BESS”) must meet the requirements set forth above in this Exhibit L (Facility Technical Requirements) Part 2 (Cybersecurity) and the following requirements regarding the ESS: 
 BESS
Units must be listed in accordance with ANSI/VAN/UL UL 9540 Standard for Safety for Energy Storage Systems and Equipment.
Battery and battery enclosures must be tested in accordance with ANSI/CAN/UL 9540A Standard for Safety for Test Method Evaluating Thermal Runaway Fire Propagation in Battery Energy Storage Systems. The test report must be accompanied by a supplemental report prepared by a registered design professional with expertise in fire protection engineering that provides interpretation of the test data in relation to the installation requirements for the energy storage system.
The installation must comply with NFPA 855 Standard for the Installation of Stationary Energy (2023 edition) in addition to state and local fire codes.
A permanent source of water for fire protection must be supplied.
Identify any redundancy, operational margins, and contingency modes within the ESS thermal management system (TMS). All operational constraints should be specified in the event of a partial or complete TMS outage. The TMS design should include redundancy or contingency plans for TMS component failures (e.g., HVAC systems, fans, or the ability to operate in a reduced capacity if a TMS component fails). 
Participant must provide all documentation and training materials required by the relevant standards, including a Hazard Mitigation Analysis (HMA) and Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA). The development of a site specific HMA requires the participation of the Seller, GPC, the OEM of the inverter, and the EPC contractor, if applicable. 
Provide detailed augmentation plan for the Facility over the PPA Term.
ESS must be appropriately sized and configured to ensure that it consistently maintains its rated nameplate instantaneous energy output capacity at the designated POI, guaranteeing that the system can reliably meet the specified energy demands and operational requirements without any degradation in performance or efficiency. ESS must be sized to maintain rated nameplate instantaneous Energy output capacity at the POI.
Inverter
BESS inverters must be capable of operating full lead and lag in both charge and discharge conditions.
Unless the inverter is fully integrated as part of the battery supplier’s product offering, proven integration experience must be provided between the inverter OEM and the battery supplier.
Inverter must be capable of providing reactive power support at zero active power, without reducing the state of charge of the battery (additional auxiliary power consumption must be from the grid). 
BESS inverters must be grid forming capable. Bidders must provide documentation demonstrating the inverter’s grid forming capability.
Inverter grid forming control points must be integrated into the Facility site control scheme, such that minimal controls retrofit will be required when GPC decides to enable grid forming features.
Facility Design
Facility engineering and design must account for BESS augmentation plan, including but not limited to site layout, block design, collection system design, aux power design, and controls design.
Battery enclosures must be spaced per UL9540A testing results, state and local code and AHJ requirements.
Backup source must be provided for the BESS auxiliary power in case of extended grid outage to maintain power to the BESS BMS, EMS, fire protection system, and thermal management system (if required).
Testing
Continuous power test, energy capacity test, and RTE test must be performed for the BESS.
Testing must be performed to demonstrate the combined output of BESS and the Renewable Resource are controlled to mitigate equipment overload.
Technology specific characterization testing must be performed. (ex. ramp rate testing).
Additional testing must be performed as required.
End-of Life Disposal / Demolition 
Description of the end-of-life disposal/recycling plan must be included.


Exhibit M – Renewable Resource PPA Amendment Overview

If a Participant offers a Bid for a Facility that will be paired with an existing Renewable Resource, Participant or the applicable PPA counterparty (“Seller”) must execute an amendment to the PPA for the Renewable Resource (“Renewable Resource PPA”) for the purpose of allowing the paired operation of the Renewable Resource and the BESS. This Exhibit M (Renewable Resource PPA Amendment Overview) outlines the conditions and revisions that GPC anticipates will be necessary.  

Conditions:
The amendment to the Renewable Resource PPA (“Amendment”) will be subject to the Commission’s approval of: (a) the PPA procured under the RFP (“BESS PPA”); and (b) the Amendment. If either of these conditions is not satisfied, either Party may terminate the Amendment.
If applicable, certain provisions of the Amendment will become effective when Seller has obtained all consents from its financing parties that are reasonably necessary for Seller’s continued performance of the Amendment.
Certain provisions of the Amendment will become effective upon the later of: (a) the date necessary financing consents are provided; and (b) the date when the BESS has achieved commercial operation pursuant to the terms of the BESS PPA. The listed revisions in item (i) below fall into this category.
Revisions:
The point of delivery under the Renewable Resource PPA (“POD”) will be moved to a new location, and Seller will deliver to the new POD energy from the Renewable Resource. GPC will have the right to dispatch the energy to either the BESS or the Point of Interconnection, and Seller will support GPC’s efforts. 
The metering system will treat the energy delivered to the POD as if it had been delivered to the POI (i.e., electrical line losses for delivery of energy to the POI will be accounted for in the meter readings).
Title to energy will pass from Seller to GPC at the POD. Risk of loss of energy will pass from Seller to: (a) the Seller entity under the BESS PPA at the POD, if energy is directed from the POD to the BESS; and (b) GPC at the POI, if energy is directed from the POD to the POI.
The operating procedures under the Renewable Resource PPA will be amended to address the incorporation of the BESS and GPC’s right to dispatch energy from the Renewable Resource to the BESS or the Point of Interconnection.
If the Renewable Resource is not currently capable of operating on AGC, Seller must install AGC consistent with the AGC requirements set out in the BESS PPA.
Seller is entitled to curtail or cease delivery of energy to the POD for a period not to exceed 30 Days so that it can connect the BESS to the substation and test and commission the BESS (such connection, the “BESS Connection” and such outage, a “BESS Connection Outage”). 
Any partial or complete outage of the Renewable Resource in connection with a BESS Connection Outage will constitute a scheduled outage approved by GPC, so long as Seller provides GPC with advance written notice of any BESS Connection Outage.
The amount of energy that Seller could have delivered to the POD but for the BESS Connection Outage (“BESS Connection Outage Energy”) will be incorporated into the Renewable Resource PPA’s frameworks for curtailment but will not be paid.
During testing and commissioning of the BESS, but before commercial operation of the BESS, energy delivered to the BESS will be: (a) separately metered and (b) paid for by GPC as though it had been delivered to the POI.
Defined terms will be revised or added, as applicable, to the Renewable Resource PPA in furtherance of the above revisions.
As applicable, exhibits describing or depicting the Renewable Resource will be deleted and replaced with updated exhibits.
